Female Sumatran rhinoceroses reach a maximum body length of 250 centimeters [Li = 250 centimeters], a dimension that reflects their status as the smallest extant rhinocerotid species. Neonates emerge weighing on average 23 kilograms [Wwb = 23 kilograms], a relatively modest birth mass given the ultimate wet weight of adult females, which exceeds 1,260 kilograms [Wwi = 1,260 kilograms]. This disparity between birth mass and adult size underscores an extended period of postnatal growth, during which the calf must more than double its initial mass within the first half-year of life. The protective behavior of mothers during the early suckling stage is crucial, as calf mortality from predation and accidents remains significant in the dense rainforest habitats of Sumatra and Borneo, where a single calf represents a considerable proportion of a female's lifetime reproductive investment given the protracted birth intervals typical of this species. The altricial nature of the newborn rhinoceros, though seemingly robust, demands continuous maternal attendance and a substantial commitment of resources even before the onset of independent foraging.

Gestation in Dicerorhinus sumatrensis is notably protracted, with a recorded gestation time of 236 days [tg = 236 days] at a maternal core body temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. This value, comparable to that of Rhinoceros unicornis, aligns with the general eutherian pattern linking prolonged gestation to large body size and is one of the key factors contributing to the slow reproductive turnover observed in the Rhinocerotidae. The interval from parturition to nutritional independence is also substantial; the time since birth at weaning has been documented at 502 days after birth [tx = 502 days after birth] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. During this extended nursing period, the suckling juvenile gradually transitions to a diet of browse, while the milk provisioning from the mother supports a steadily increasing body mass, allowing the calf to grow from an initial 23 kilograms to nearly 906 kilograms by the time it achieves full dietary independence.

The life-history pace of the Sumatran rhinoceros is characteristically slow. Recorded lifespan in the wild and in managed care reaches approximately 32.8 years [am = approximately 32.8 years], an estimate derived from longitudinal observations at a stable body temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. This extensive longevity, combined with late reproductive maturation, results in a limited number of reproductive opportunities per individual across its lifetime. Females do not attain puberty until approximately 7.5 years after birth, a delayed onset that is characteristic of large-bodied mammalian herbivores and which places considerable demographic pressure on populations already reduced by poaching and habitat loss. The extended period of somatic growth preceding sexual maturation likely reflects the necessity of reaching the substantial body mass required for successful parturition and subsequent lactation, two highly demanding physiological processes under eutherian metabolism.

Female calves, under the thermal regime of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C], do not reach puberty until approximately 2,738 days after birth [tp = approximately 2,738 days after birth], whereas males mature noticeably earlier, at roughly 1,643 days after birth. The maximum reproductive output under optimal captive conditions is constrained by this delayed maturation and the long inter-birth interval. The maximum reproductive rate for females, measured at 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C], is estimated at one offspring every 1,278 days [Ri = one offspring every 1,278 days], a value that reflects the combined constraints of a 502-day weaning period after birth (502 days after birth) [tx = 502 days after birth] and the physiological demands of maternal condition recovery. This spacing between successive calves naturally limits the lifetime fecundity of any given female, making each breeding event critically important to overall population persistence.

At weaning, calves typically weigh approximately 905.6 kilograms [Wwx = approximately 905.6 kilograms], representing a substantial proportion of the adult body weight of around 1,260 kilograms [Wwi = around 1,260 kilograms]. This high weaning mass provides the growing juvenile with a significant energy reserve as it becomes nutritionally independent and begins foraging on its own, transitioning from milk-dependent young to a fully herbivorous sub-adult. The dietary transition involves a gradual shift from maternal milk to a varied intake of leaves, twigs, and fruit characteristic of their dense lowland forest environment. This stage is critical for building the skeletal frame and muscle mass necessary for future survival, as the individual must now compete with conspecifics for food resources while navigating a habitat increasingly fragmented by human activity. The body length of adult females, typically reaching 250 centimeters [Li = 250 centimeters], combined with the substantial mass at weaning, equips the young rhinoceros with a size advantage that minimizes predation risk as it enters the sub-adult stage.
